summary:
Earth’s surface never stops moving, but the changes that matter are often invisible from space, hidden under cloud, night or snow. Surface Dance is an open-source web application that reads surface change from NISAR L-band radar by putting two dates under one slider.

We study the Ciénaga Grande de Santa Marta, Colombia’s largest coastal lagoon: a Ramsar wetland with documented mangrove mortality, on a coast optical satellites rarely see clearly because it is almost permanently clouded. Radar does not care about cloud, and water’s very high dielectric constant makes it unmistakable to an L-band pulse.

Drag the handle and the map wipes between 22 June and 20 October 2026, both scenes from NISAR pass 119, frame 007, dual-polarization. Switch channel and the same place answers a different question: HH darkens over open water and brightens where the pulse double-bounces between flooded trunks, while HV listens for volume scattering from canopy. Change is computed as 10*log10(after/before), because radar backscatter is multiplicative, and every scene carries its processing collection and CRID.

We show where the surface danced, and we say plainly where we cannot tell.
details:
What it does

Surface Dance turns two NISAR radar acquisitions of the same place into something a non-specialist can read in ten seconds. The map holds both dates at once; dragging a handle wipes between them. A second mode replaces the wipe with a change layer, where every pixel reports how much the radar echo rose or fell between the two dates, in decibels. A third mode groups the change into types. An AI summary restates the numbers in plain English and Spanish, and a question panel answers a fixed set of team-written questions about what the page shows.

What we found

Both scenes come from pass 119 ascending, frame 007, collection PROVISIONAL, CRID P05023, 120 days apart, with six seconds between overpass times. Against that baseline the HH echo grew by 3 dB or more across 20.4% of the scene and faded across 3.6%, median shift +0.64 dB. The cross-polarized HV channel barely moved: 1.7% and 2.0%, median +0.42 dB. Open water went from 329.5 to 344 km², +4.4%, on an Otsu threshold of -15.2 and -13.7 dB.

Stratifying by what each pixel was in the first scene, 95% of the rise is on surfaces that were open water in June: median +2.41 dB with 44.0% above 3 dB, against +0.20 dB and 1.7% on land. The headline is therefore narrow and specific: the water surface changed, and the lagoon did not grow.

We then tested our own explanation and lost it. Wind roughening predicts a brighter surface, so we checked NASA POWER at both overpass hours: 2.97 m/s on 22 June against 0.87 m/s on 20 October. The brighter date had 3.4 times less wind, the opposite of the prediction, and we discarded regional wind. The caveat we state rather than hide is that NASA POWER resolves wind on a ~50 km cell, so a local breeze below that cell, rain at the overpass hour and very shallow water all remain open. Separating depth from roughness and moisture needs water surface elevation, a local wind record, and the full twelve-day NISAR stack rather than two dates. Nine granules exist on this track and frame; cycles 026 and 027 are missing because the instrument did not acquire between 28 July and 9 August 2026.

How it works

We use NISAR Level-2 GCOV products, which are geocoded and terrain-corrected, so the two dates land on the same grid without us reprojecting anything. Both scenes come from the same pass, the same frame and the same processing collection, because two acquisitions seen from different look angles would produce a difference map of the geometry rather than of the ground. Speckle is suppressed with a boxcar filter before comparison, and the window size is recorded in the metadata and shown in the interface, since smoothing trades spatial detail for confidence and the reader deserves to know which they are looking at. Change is computed as 10*log10(after/before): a ratio rather than a subtraction, because radar backscatter is multiplicative. Every layer ships with a metadata file carrying the product collection, the CRID, both acquisition dates, the geographic bounds, the filter parameters, the display range and the percentage of pixels that rose or fell beyond a stated threshold.

Why polarization is the heart of it

The challenge asks which polarizations reveal change on land and ice, and the answer is that they ask different questions of the same ground. HH is co-polarized: open water returns almost nothing and appears dark, but flooded vegetation can appear brilliantly bright, because the pulse bounces off the water surface and again off the trunks before returning. HV is cross-polarized and responds to volume scattering from canopy and structurally complex surfaces. Switching channels in the application over the same wetland makes the distinction visible rather than theoretical: a pixel that darkens in HH and holds steady in HV is telling a different story from one that darkens in both. In our scenes that contrast is the whole argument: HH moved twelve times more than HV, which is what rules out a new canopy and points the signal at the surface.

Why this place

The Ciénaga Grande de Santa Marta is Colombia's largest coastal lagoon and a Ramsar wetland with a documented history of hydrological alteration and mangrove mortality. It also sits under one of the cloudiest skies in the Caribbean, which means optical monitoring is intermittent at exactly the moments when flooding matters. That is not a limitation we worked around; it is the argument for radar, and it is why this site rewards NISAR rather than merely tolerating it. It is Ramsar Site 951, designated 18 June 1998, 400,000 hectares, also a UNESCO Biosphere Reserve, and the fishing ground of the stilt villages built on its water. It is governed nationally and reported into international frameworks, so free, cloud-proof, repeatable evidence changes who can take part in the argument about it.

What we do not claim

NISAR's public archive opens in October 2025, so this is change between two dates and nothing resembling a climate trend. A change in backscatter is a change in roughness or moisture: that is evidence about the surface, not a direct measurement of flooding, deforestation or mangrove loss, and we label interpretation as interpretation. We decline to quantify change across different processing collections, because the result would be an artefact of the algorithm. The application also ships a clearly banner-marked synthetic demo for testing the interface, which is labelled as invented data on every screen so that no viewer can mistake it for an observation.

Tools

Python for the processing pipeline, reading the GCOV products with h5py and writing web layers with rasterio and GDAL, with NumPy and Matplotlib; scikit-learn for the k-means used by Change types. A plain JavaScript front end with Leaflet for the map and no build step, so the whole application is auditable by reading the source; Hugging Face transformers.js loads a small open sentence model in the viewer's browser for the question panel. Tests run under Playwright in GitHub Actions, and the site is published with GitHub Pages. Everything is open-source licensed in a public repository. No paid services and no proprietary data. The project follows the practice taught in NASA's Open Science 101 material and NASA ARSET's applications guidance: an open repository under MIT, every published layer shipped with the metadata needed to reproduce it, the processing commands given in the README, and stated uncertainty rather than a single confident number.

Creativity

Our team is called Los Bailarines del SAR, and this challenge describes Earth's surface as an endless dance. We took that as a design brief rather than a joke: the interface is built entirely around movement between two moments, and the slider is the instrument. The restraint is deliberate too. The obvious move is to train a classifier and announce a prediction; we instead built something transparent enough that a reader can disagree with us using our own numbers, which are printed beside the map rather than buried in a repository. The clearest example is the wind test: we had a tidy explanation, we measured it, it failed, and we published the failure.

Use of AI, and where exactly

Parts of this repository were written with the assistance of AI coding tools, an AI assistant executed the project's own processing pipeline on the NISAR granules to generate the published layers, and the synthetic demonstration scenes under ?demo=1 were generated programmatically to test the interface. The demo is labelled as invented data on every screen and contains no NISAR observation. All method choices, polarization selections, masking rules, thresholds and scientific interpretations were specified, reviewed and approved by the human team members named in this submission. No NISAR scene, measurement, result or figure presented as an observation was generated, synthesised or altered by an AI tool.

Three components of the application are machine-generated and labelled as such in the interface. Change types are produced by unsupervised k-means clustering over the HH and HV change values; the clustering groups pixels by similarity and assigns no physical meaning, and the class names are written by the team from visible rules. Read the dance, the plain-language summary, is written by a language model (Claude Opus 5.5) from numbers the pipeline already computed, recorded in web/layers/cienaga/summary.json under generated_with; it restates computed values in English and Spanish and introduces no new figure. Ask the radar answers a fixed set of team-written questions; a small open model (paraphrase-multilingual-MiniLM-L12-v2, Apache-2.0) running in the viewer's browser matches a free question to the closest of those answers and never writes text, and what the viewer types stays on their device. None of the three predicts flooding, damage or any future state.

The text of the 7-slide demo deck was also drafted with AI assistance. No image in the application or in the deck was generated by AI; every figure is pipeline output, a screenshot of the application, or the unaltered NASA Space Apps Challenge logo.
